sections.title: DIPHTHERIA
paragraphs: Etiopathogenesis Cause: Infection by Corynebacterium diphtheriae.
Necrotic changes in respiratory tract mucous membranes.
Damage to heart muscle and nervous system.
Clinical Symptoms Gray, fibrinous exudates (bleed when removed):
Tonsils, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, ears, skin (rarely).
Fever, malaise, sore throat, neck muscle swelling.
Sore throat, high fever, difficulty swallowing, soft tissue swelling, cardiac conduction disorders.
Hoarseness, cough, breathlessness, respiratory difficulties (multiple complications).
Diagnosis: Based on clinical picture. Symptoms depend on infection site.
GFE (Gray Fibrinous Exudates) on Tonsils, Pharynx, Larynx, Trachea, Bronchi, Ears, Skin.
Key Dose: 10–14 days of ampicillin/erythromycin for chemoprophylaxis.
Diagnosis Tip: Clinical picture is the primary diagnostic criterion for diphtheria.

Progressive increase in muscle tone in the neck, back, abdomen, and limbs (mainly lower limbs)

sections.title: Etiopathogenesis
paragraphs: Condition in which the proximal segment of the intestine, following peristaltic movement, telescopes into a more distal segment. Antiperistaltic invagination is rare.
80% of cases involve children aged 4–12 months; occurs significantly more often in boys.
Most commonly leads to small bowel intussusception in the ileum.
95% of cases have no identifiable cause. Contributing factors include:
Anatomical factors: Meckel’s diverticulum, intestinal polyps, jejunal diverticula Post-infectious ileitis: Enlargement of Peyer’s patches
Respiratory tract infection or diarrhea: Adenovirus!
Central peritonitis: In the course of Schoenlein-Henoch syndrome Cholelithiasis, neoplastic masses

sections.title: Clinical Symptoms Pediatrics
paragraphs: Sudden attacks with periods of colicky abdominal pain.
Vomits containing bile, followed by intestinal contents.
Stools with a mixture of bloody mucus ("mucoid currant jelly") and fresh blood.
Tender, movable mass of the intussuscepted intestine
Variable peristaltic pattern: Metallic tones, high-pitched during pain attacks, silent between attacks
Right lower quadrant of the abdomen appears empty
Blood in stool on rectal examination 🧠Memory Aid
- Treatment: Air enema (first-line) or surgery Key Statistics:

- Cause: 95% idiopathic; 5% secondary (e.g., Meckel’s diverticulum, Peyer’s patches) Comparison Table: Common Causes of Intussusception | Cause | Examples | |-------------------------|---------------------------------------| | Anatomical | Meckel’s diverticulum, polyps | | Post-infectious | Enlarged Peyer’s patches | | Infectious | Adenovirus, Schoenlein-Henoch syndrome| | Others | Cholelithiasis, neoplasms |
- "Currant jelly" stool is a hallmark of intussusception.
- Air enema is the gold standard diagnostic and therapeutic intervention.

sections.title: Diagnostics
paragraphs: Surface abdominal X-ray in upright position (distention of bowel loops, fluid levels in case of bowel obstruction, signs of bowel perforation).
Ultrasound of the abdominal cavity (target image).

sections.title: Treatment
paragraphs: Combating the symptoms of shock, correcting water, electrolyte, protein, and blood count deficiencies; insertion of a gastric tube.

Conservative treatment (possible in the first 12 hours if there are no symptoms of peritonitis and the infant's general condition is good) – attempt to debulk the intestine with intrarectal infusion of a contrast medium under X-ray guidance.
Rectal enema is only performed in the early stages of the disease; later on, there is a risk of intestinal perforation.

Surgical treatment – more than 12 hours after the onset of disease symptoms, in the case of symptoms of intestinal perforation and after an unsuccessful attempt at conservative removal of the bowel; a manual removal maneuver is undertaken, and if unsuccessful or necrotic intestinal lesions are detected, resection of the pathologically changed section is performed with end-to-end anastomosis.

sections.title: Diarrhea
paragraphs: Acute diarrhea – a condition characterized by a child passing an increased number of stools per day (3 or more stools with formula feeding and 6 or more stools with breastfeeding) with an abnormal consistency or with stool(s) containing blood, pus, or mucus. Acute diarrhea lasts 10–14 days, but usually up to 7 days.
A breastfed baby may pass stool after each feeding.

Chronic diarrhea – a condition lasting more than 14 days, characterized by the child passing an increased number of 🧠Memory Aid 🧠Mnemonics for Diarrhea Classification Acute: Abdominal pain, Chronic: Continuous symptoms.
Conservative first (12 hours): Intrarectal contrast infusion.
🧠Comparison Table: Acute vs. Chronic Diarrhea Feature Acute Diarrhea Chronic Diarrhea Duration <14 days (usually ≤7 days) >14 days
Common causes Infection, dietary changes Malabsorption, chronic disease
Key diagnostic clue Blood, pus, or mucus in stool
Rectal enema is contraindicated after 12 hours due to perforation risk.

paragraphs: Definition: Presence of blood in the digestive tract, manifesting through vomit and/or stool with blood admixture.

Systemic disease-related bleeding: Bleeding throughout the entire digestive tract (e.g., hemorrhagic rash, intracranial syndrome, hemolytic- uremic syndrome, neoplastic diseases).

sections.title: Urinary Tract Infections in Children
paragraphs: Prioritize appropriate drug selection (symptomatic drugs, antivirals, anti-inflammatories, chemotherapeutics, antibiotics).
Antibiotic choice must be evidence-based, considering local epidemiology and pathogen resistance patterns.
- Diet and activity are foundational in preventing kidney stones; pharmacotherapy must be tailored to the stone type.
- Antibiotic stewardship is critical in UTIs—always consider local resistance patterns.

Urinary tract infections (UTIs) constitute 10–20% of all community-acquired infections (second only to respiratory infections in terms of frequency) and approximately 40–50% of hospital-acquired infections.

In the neonatal period and in the first quarter of life, boys are more often affected due to the higher incidence of urinary tract defects; outside this period, with the age of the child, the number of cases systematically increases among girls (the urethra is shorter and wider, located close to the anus).

sections.title: Etiopathogenesis
paragraphs: Neonatal and early infancy period: UTI occurs via the hematogenous route
Outside this period: UTI most often develops via the ascending route (from the gastrointestinal tract – Enterobacteriaceae, from the sub-preputial area – Proteus mirabilis)

Urinary tract defects (posterior urethral valve in boys, stenosis of the external urethral opening in girls), vesicoureteral reflux, neurogenic bladder Catheterization, urinary tract instrumentation

paragraphs: Bacteriological examination of urine – Findings include significant bacteriuria with assessment of drug sensitivity of cultured pathogens:

Invasive tests (supralipocentesis, catheterization) are used only in exceptional circumstances.

- Swelling and lymphadenopathy are hallmark signs in 90% of OPKZN cases.
- Monitor blood pressure changes in lymphadenopathy cases.

sections.title: Clinical Presentation
paragraphs: Onset: 1 day to 2–3 weeks; rarely signs of encephalopathy with hypertension (symptoms: severe headaches, nausea, vomiting, visual disturbances, tremors, difficulty swallowing).
Occurs in ~30% of cases; lasts up to 2 weeks, then progresses to hemoglobinuria (characteristic of OPKZN), which may persist for 6–12 months.
Complications: Hemoglobinuria and anemia → acute kidney failure with hyperazotemia, hyperkalemia, and metabolic acidosis.

sections.title: Laboratory Diagnostics
paragraphs: Hematuria with fresh and degenerated RBCs (often dysmorphic RBCs on contrast-enhanced microscopy).
Proteinuria: Unstable sign of OPKZN; rarely <3 g/24 hours (mainly albuminuria), rarely leading to nephrotic syndrome.
Leukocyturia: Present primarily in early illness (alkaline urine).
Crystalline and granular casts: Seen in severe proteinuria (present in all OPKZN cases).
↑ ASO titer (peaks 4–6 weeks after OPKZN) in all OPKZN patients, after glomerulonephritis, and in ~50% of patients with skin inflammation.
↑ IgG (>50% of cases), ↑ IgA (~30% of cases).
C3 and total hemolytic complement activity.

sections.title: Treatment Memory Aid
paragraphs: Bed rest: Continue until swelling, hypertension, and hematuria resolve.
Penicillamine: 50–100 mg/kg/day (divided into 3–4 doses; max 3 g/day for 10 days).
Infants <2 months: 15–50 mg/kg/day (3–4 divided doses) or cephalosporins.

sections.title: Mnemonic for OPKZN (Post-streptococcal Glomerulonephritis)
paragraphs: Opening: Onset 1–3 weeks after strep infection.
Zn: Zn (not a mnemonic—OPKZN is a Polish acronym for "nephritis post-infection streptococcal").

sections.title: Key Lab Findings in OPKZN
paragraphs: Parameter Finding Complement C3 ↓ (key diagnostic marker) ASO titer ↑ (peaks 4–6 weeks post-infection) Proteinuria <3 g/24h (unlike nephrotic syndrome) RBC morphology Dysmorphic RBCs (not intact)

sections.title: Clinical Pearl
paragraphs: Hemoglobinuria (not hematuria) is a hallmark of OPKZN, distinguishing it from other glomerulonephritides.

sections.title: Liquification of Inflammatory Foci
paragraphs: Occurs in the nasal-pharyngeal cavity, nasopharynx, and sinuses.

sections.title: Dietary Recommendations
paragraphs: Limit fluid intake and salt consumption (depending on edema and body mass).
Reduce protein content in the diet (in cases of hyperazotemia).
Limit potassium-containing products (in cases of hyperkalemia).

sections.title: Acute Renal Failure
paragraphs: In a small number of cases, dialysis is required.

~1% of children develop chronic kidney insufficiency or persistent hematuria.
May lead to sclerosing glomerulonephritis, hypertension, and reduced proteinuria (hypocomplementemia lasting >6 months).

paragraphs: - Measure CT during every doctor visit.

- Use of medications that may increase CT
- Diseases that can progress with NT (neurological deterioration?)

sections.title: Measurement Protocol
paragraphs: Avoid stimulants and drinks before examination.
Child should sit calmly for 5 minutes before measurement.
Child sits with back supported, feet on the floor, right arm at heart level.
Cuff should cover 80–100% of arm circumference.
Cuff width must be ≥ 40% of arm circumference.
Too narrow cuffs increase measurement errors.
Compare CT results with normative centile grids for sex, age, and height.
Classification of arterial hypertension depends on sex, age, and height.

sections.title: Stage I Hypertension

If reduced blood pressure persists during two subsequent measurements:
Refer to a relevant center within one month
Internal organ damage (heart, kidneys, retinas, blood vessels) Type I or II diabetes

sections.title: Stage II Hypertension

Start diagnostic procedures or refer to a relevant center within one week (immediately if symptomatic)

sections.title: Severe Hypertension
paragraphs: Condition where systolic blood pressure exceeds 99th percentile for age by at least 30 mmHg.

sections.title: Sudden and Urgent Hypertensive States Diagnosis of Hypertension

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Second most common solid tumor after OUN tumors in children, accounting for 8% of all childhood cancers.
Most commonly occurs in infants and toddlers.
Most common aggressive tumor during the neonatal period and most common abdominal mass up to 3 years of age.
Most frequent localization: 75% abdominal cavity (retroperitoneal space and adrenal glands).
Origin: Develops from nerve cells that give rise to sympathetic nerves and adrenal glands.
Spontaneous regression tendency in the neonatal period.

sections.title: Clinical Symptoms
paragraphs: Depend on location and stage of primary tumor spread.
Homer sign: Drooping eyelid, sunken eyeball, constricted pupil, iris discoloration on the affected side.
Respiratory symptoms: Dyspnea, respiratory tract infections, swallowing difficulties.
Gastrointestinal symptoms: Loss of appetite, nausea, abdominal pain.
Abdominal findings: Enlarged abdominal mass (often with kidney involvement).
Rectal findings: Rectal palpable mass, rectal discharge.
Localized back pain, weakened lower extremities, muscle weakness.
Skin discoloration, rash, increased reflexes, scoliosis.
Urinary incontinence, external urethral obstruction, lack of sweating.
Encephalopathy: Ataxia, myoclonus, opsomyoclonus (chaotic, variable oculomotor).
Gastrointestinal effects: Diarrhea due to intestinal atony (VIP secretion increase).
Sudden flushing with excessive sweating (catecholamine secretion increase).
Protruding eyeball, ocular discharge, swelling of eyelids and eyebrows.
- Diarrhea (VIP secretion) 🧠Clinical Pearls VIP (vasoactive intestinal peptide) secretion causes diarrhea and intestinal atony.
Catecholamine excess leads to flushing, sweating, and tachycardia.
Homer sign is a classic indicator of adrenal or retroperitoneal neuroblastoma.
Neuroblastoma is the most common abdominal tumor in children under 3 years.

sections.title: Contraindications to Protective Vaccinations
paragraphs: The current immunization schedule for mandatory and recommended vaccines (updated annually) is available on the websites of health and epidemiological stations.

sections.title: Factual Contraindications to Vaccination
paragraphs: 1. Acute infectious diseases or exacerbation of chronic illness.
2. Severe congenital or acquired immune deficiencies – vaccination against live vaccines (measles, mumps, rubella, chickenpox).
3. Blood transfusion or immunoglobulin preparations – contraindicated in relation to live vaccines for 3–6 months following administration.
4. Documented severe allergic reactions of anaphylactic type after a previous dose of the same vaccine or evidence of identical reaction to any component of that vaccine.
5. Progressive neurological diseases, congenital metabolic disorders with central nervous system damage, children undergoing neurodevelopmental assessment.
6. Body weight below 2000 g and children born before 32 weeks gestation – contraindicated for measles vaccination.
7. Exercise great caution in the administration of vaccines in cases of children with autoimmune diseases – use an individualized immunization schedule.

sections.title: States and Conditions Not Constituting Contraindications to Vaccination (According to WHO) Memory Aid
paragraphs: 1. Upper respiratory tract infections or diarrhea with a temperature below 38.5°C and other non-progressive signs of infection.
2. Allergy, asthma (without exacerbation), or other symptoms of atopic dermatitis, rhinitis, or nasal congestion.
6. Family history indicating the presence of allergies in the family.
7. Antibiotic therapy, low doses of steroids or local application (e.g., on the skin or locally).
8. Skin inflammation, rash, or localized skin infection.

sections.title: Mnemonic for Factual Contraindications

sections.title: Clinical Pearls Congenital and Acquired Infections
paragraphs: Live vaccines (e.g., MMR, varicella) are contraindicated in severe immune deficiencies.
Wait 3–6 months after blood transfusion/immunoglobulin before administering live vaccines.
Mild illnesses (e.g., colds, diarrhea without fever) do not contraindicate vaccination.
Autoimmune diseases require individualized schedules – not absolute contraindications.

sections.title: 2. Ductal-Dependent Systemic Flow Defects
paragraphs: These defects impede left ventricular outflow. Systemic circulation relies on right-to-left blood flow through the ductus arteriosus.
a. Critical aortic stenosis (AS) b. Critical coarctation of the aorta (CoA) c. Interrupted aortic arch (IAA) d. Hypoplastic left heart syndrome (HLHS)

- Condition deteriorates within 2–3 days due to ductus closure.
- Presents with generalized central cyanosis, hypoxemia, hypoxia, and metabolic acidosis.
2. Neonate appears normal for several hours after birth.
3. Rapid deterioration occurs with ductus closure.

sections.title: HYPOGLYCEMIA
paragraphs: This is a decrease in blood glucose levels. In breastfed infants for the first 3 hours after birth, the lowest glucose level should be > 35 mg%, by the end of the first day > 40 mg%, and during the first week of life > 45 mg%.
Hypoglycemia in the neonatal period can lead to damage to the central nervous system!

sections.title: Factors Increasing Risk of Hypoglycemia in Newborns:
Clinical Symptoms
paragraphs: The symptoms of hypoglycemia in newborns are non-characteristic and may be subtle. Therefore, all infants at risk should have their blood glucose levels checked depending on the results and condition of the child: every 6 hours during the first day, every 12 hours during the second day, and every
The symptoms of hypoglycemia in infants are also non-specific. They may include apathy, hypotonia, lethargy, tremors, jaundice, hypothermia, and respiratory disturbances.
Mnemonic for hypoglycemia risk factors: Prematurity, IUGR, Excessive weight, Maternal diabetes, Aspyxia, Cold, Infection, Heart defects,
Clinical pearl: Non-specific symptoms (e.g., lethargy, tremors) necessitate routine glucose monitoring in high-risk infants to prevent CNS damage.

sections.title: Hypoglycemia in Neonatal Period
paragraphs: Hypoglycemia occurring during the neonatal period is part of Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome (hypoglycemia, large birth weight, umbilical hernia, hepatosplenomegaly, adrenal cortex cell hypertrophy, increased susceptibility to embryonal tumors – e.g., neuroblastoma, Wilms tumor, hepatoblastoma, rhabdomyosarcoma [enlarged tongue]), which should be excluded during physical examination.

sections.title: GALACTOSEMIA (galactosaemia)
paragraphs: This is an autosomal recessive genetic disorder caused by the inability to convert galactose into glucose.
Frequency of clinically significant, classic galactosemia: 1:35,000.
Caused by mutations in the gene responsible for the correct function of galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase (GALT).
Newborns initially healthy after first milk feeding develop:
Rapidly increasing vomiting, diarrhea, jaundice, liver and spleen enlargement, coagulation disorders, acidosis, hypoglycemia, glucosuria.
Untreated disease leads to mental retardation, intellectual disability, and persistent liver insufficiency.
Galactose levels elevated in milk and urine.
Lack of GALT activity in erythrocytes (test performed on dried blood; not part of routine screening).
Bilirubin elevation with separation into free (indirect) and conjugated (direct) fractions.
- Testing: erythrocyte GALT activity, galactose in urine Clinical Pearls:
- Classic symptoms of galactosemia: vomiting, diarrhea, jaundice, and liver enlargement.
- Key diagnostic tests: GALT activity in erythrocytes, galactose in urine, and bilirubin fractionation.
- Untreated consequences: irreversible intellectual disability and liver failure.

sections.title: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn (PPHN) Pediatric Diagnostics and Treatment
paragraphs: Definition A clinical syndrome manifesting early after birth, characterized by persistent right-to-left shunting through the patent ductus arteriosus and foramen ovale, causing severe oxygenation disorders in the newborn.
Occurs in 1:1000 to 1:1400 live-born infants Etiopathogenesis
Pathogenic factors disrupt normal relaxation of pulmonary vascular smooth muscle post-birth
Persistent high pulmonary vascular resistance → pulmonary hypertension → right ventricular strain → increased shunting through ductus arteriosus and patent foramen ovale Clinical Symptoms
Cyanosis unresponsive to oxygen therapy Tachypnea (accelerated breathing)
PPHN cyanosis does not improve with oxygen – distinguish from other causes of neonatal cyanosis (e.g., tetralogy of Fallot).

paragraphs: Definition: A lung segment separated from the bronchial tree and pulmonary arteries, forming an isolated, non-functional fragment.

Connection to bronchial tree: Infection, abscess, empyema.
Radiographic findings: Thickening and mottling in the affected area.
Diagnosis: Aortography shows occlusion of pulmonary arteries.

sections.title: the newborn)
paragraphs: This is a severe and life-threatening condition caused by an immunological reaction between maternal IgG antibodies and fetal red blood cell antigens in the ABO, Rh system, and less commonly Kidd, Kell, Duffy, and Lewis.
As a result of this disease, there is destruction of fetal and neonatal red blood cells leading to anemia, jaundice with severe consequences potentially damaging the central nervous system.

sections.title: Epidemiology
paragraphs: Hemolytic disease may appear in the first pregnancy without previous sensitization but has a milder course compared to Rh-incompatibility hemolytic disease.

sections.title: Etiopathogenesis
paragraphs: Maternal antibodies are formed due to early fetal red blood cell passage into maternal circulation during childbirth, spontaneous or induced abortion, and as a result of group incompatible blood transfusion.
Only IgG antibodies play a pathogenic role in the serological conflict because they have the ability to cross the placental barrier.

sections.title: Clinical Symptoms Hemolytic Disease of the Newborn
paragraphs: Hemolytic anemia Hyperbilirubinemia (increased unconjugated bilirubin due to red blood cell breakdown) Hepatosplenomegaly
Severe jaundice (conjugated bilirubin level over 20 mg/dL or increasing conjugated bilirubin > 0.5 mg/kg mc./hour)
- ABO, Rh, Kidd, Kell, Duffy, Lewis → Remember as "ARKKDL" (first letters of systems involved in hemolytic disease).
Comparison Table: ABO vs. Rh Incompatibility Feature ABO Incompatibility Rh Incompatibility Onset
Usually second or later pregnancies Severity Mild Severe Antibody Type IgG IgG Common Complication
Severe anemia, fetal edema Clinical Pearl:
- IgG antibodies are the only pathogenic antibodies in hemolytic disease because they cross the placenta.
- Conjugated bilirubin > 20 mg/dL is a critical threshold for severe jaundice in neonates.

sections.title: Diagnostics
paragraphs: In Rh incompatibility, erythroblasts are demonstrated.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Caused by IgG antibodies from the mother reacting with fetal red blood cell antigens in the ABO, Rh, Kidd, Kell, Duffy, and Lewis systems.

sections.title: Epidemiology

Rh system: Conflict typically occurs only during the second pregnancy (first pregnancy has an immunizing effect).

Spontaneous or induced abortion Non-group-compatible blood transfusion

Hemolytic anemia Jaundice (elevated unconjugated bilirubin – indirect, from red blood cell breakdown)

sections.title: Wrodzona Niedoczynność Tarczycy
paragraphs: (hypothyreosis congenita, hypothyroidism congenita, congenital hypothyroidism) A disorder of physical and intellectual development caused by the deficiency of thyroid hormones during pregnancy and in newborns.

sections.title: Epidemiology
paragraphs: Wrodzona niedoczynność tarczycy występuje u noworodków z częstością 1:4000.

sections.title: Etiopathogenesis
paragraphs: Thyroid hormones are the most important factor controlling normal physical and mental development. From the third month of pregnancy, fetal thyroid begins to produce its own hormones. In case of their deficiency, central nervous system development is delayed. Neonatal hypothyroidism is characterized by:
- Elevated (or within normal limits) TSH level
- Reduced levels of fT3 and fT4
1. Anomalies in thyroid development (hypoplasia, aplasia, dysgenesis, ectopia)
2. Iodine deficiency (supplementation for pregnant women during pregnancy and breastfeeding)
3. Unbalanced maternal hypothyroidism (maternal treatment is necessary)
5. Defects in the synthesis of thyroid hormones

sections.title: Clinical Symptoms Congenital Hypothyroidism in Pediatrics
paragraphs: Clinical symptoms appear only in the first weeks of life (transplacental passage of maternal thyroid hormones) 🧠Memory Aid Key Points for Congenital Hypothyroidism:
Critical time for thyroid hormone impact: Third trimester of pregnancy

Early detection: Newborn screening (TSH/fT4 levels) Management: Lifelong levothyroxine replacement (dose adjusted based on age and weight) Comparison Table: Causes vs. Management | Cause | Management | |-----------------------------------|---------------------------------------------| | Iodine deficiency | Maternal iodine supplementation | | Thyroid developmental anomalies | Levothyroxine replacement |

| Maternal hypothyroidism | Maternal thyroid hormone treatment | | Autoimmune/inflammatory processes | Levothyroxine replacement | | Enzymatic defects | Levothyroxine replacement | | Resistance to thyroid hormones | Higher levothyroxine doses, regular monitoring |

sections.title: Definition and Overview
paragraphs: DDH refers to various abnormalities of the hip joint in infants and children.
Characterized by a tendency for spontaneous improvement or worsening over time.
Most common cause: inadequate positioning of the femoral head and improper modeling of the acetabular roof.
Untreated DDH leads to hip joint dislocation.
Modern terminology replaces "congenital dysplasia of the hip," emphasizing that hip joint development can occur even in infancy.

sections.title: Etiopathogenesis
paragraphs: - Anteversion and stiffness of the femoral head.
- Thinness and collapse of the acetabular roof.

sections.title: Contributing Factors
paragraphs: - Increased risk if dysplasia occurs in parents or offspring.
- Estrogens relax ligaments and joint capsules.
- Higher estrogen sensitivity in females explains increased prevalence in female infants.
- Obstetric/neonatal procedures (e.g., manual assistance during delivery, birth asphyxia resuscitation).
🧠Memory Aid 🧠Mnemonic for Etiopathogenesis Factors: GGH I Genetic (family history).
🧠Clinical Pearl DDH is more common in females due to hormonal influences (estrogen) and anatomical differences in pelvic structure.
Early detection (via physical exam and imaging) is critical to prevent long-term joint damage.
Teratogenic DDH is rare but often linked to intrauterine constraints (e.g., oligohydramnios, fetal crowding).

paragraphs: Early detection: Multiple delicate examinations during pregnancy and up to 1 year after birth. First examination should occur at the beginning of childhood.

Child placed on their side with hips abducted

sections.title: Key Diagnostic Criteria Treatment Approach
paragraphs: Pathological dislocations: Structural abnormalities, congenital conditions (e.g., myelodysplasia, arthrogryposis).
Post-inflammatory dislocations: Result from joint inflammation or trauma.
Teratogenic dislocations: Caused by maternal exposure to teratogens (e.g., alcohol, drugs).
Congenital systemic diseases: Associated with systemic disorders (e.g., Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Larsen syndrome).

sections.title: 1. Immediate Postnatal Management
paragraphs: Goal: Prolong the transition period of the joint from fetal to extended position.
Joint positioning: Place the joint in a fetal-like position to ensure congruence.
Method: Extensive swaddling immediately after birth.

sections.title: 2. Infants ≤ 6 Months of Age
paragraphs: First-line treatment: Pavlik harness (lowest risk of femoral head necrosis).

sections.title: 3. Infants > 6 Months or Pavlik Harness Failure
paragraphs: Recommended: Closed reduction with adductor tenotomy, followed by immobilization in a cast.

sections.title: 4. Children > 18 Months or Failed Closed Reduction
paragraphs: Referral: Surgical treatment (e.g., open reduction, osteotomy).

sections.title: 1. Adrenaline
paragraphs: Mechanism of action: Catecholamine that acts on β1 and β2 receptors; higher doses also activate alpha receptors.
Intratracheal administration: Requires several times higher doses. Dilute with saline to a volume of 1–2 ml.
Side effects: Excessively increased heart rate, decreased coronary perfusion, vomiting.

sections.title: 2. Sodium Bicarbonate (8.4% NaHCO₃)
paragraphs: Mechanism of action: Alkalization by buffering H⁺.
Use restrictions: Only in properly ventilated neonates. Only if metabolic acidosis is suspected.
Dose: Calculated from formula: 0.3 × weight × base deficiency. In resuscitation: 2–4 ml/kg body weight.
Side effects: Disturbances of acid-base balance, increased blood osmolarity, extravasation causes tissue necrosis.

sections.title: 3. Naloxone Hydrochloride (Narcan)
paragraphs: Mechanism of action: Antagonist with no agonist activity for natural and synthetic analgesics.
ABC: Acts on Alpha, Beta, and Cardiac receptors.
Dilute: Always dilute to 1–2 ml for intratracheal use.
BASIC: Used for Bicarbonate in Acidosis, Slow infusion, In ventilated neonates, Calculation-based dosing.
Avoid: Never use without proper ventilation.
NARCAN: Remember the Name and Route (IV/ET).
Seizures: Risk of Seizures with overdose.

sections.title: MEASLES (MORBILLI)
paragraphs: Transmission via droplets, the source is an infected person.
Incubation period – 4 days before and 3 days after the rash appears.
- Fever up to 39°C, dry cough, runny nose, sore throat, conjunctivitis, redness of the eyelids, photophobia;

- Koplik's spots appear in the 2nd or 3rd day of the pre-rash phase – white spots with a red border localized on the buccal mucosa of the mouth at the height of the lower incisors and premolars, preceding the rash by 1–2 days.
- Lasts 3–4 days; fever up to 40°C, worsening general condition;
- Small, erythematous spots that later become papules localized mainly behind the ears along the hairline, quickly spread over the face and trunk, showing a tendency to merge.
🧠Memory Aid Koplik's Spots Mnemonic: Before Rash, Buccal Mucosa, Red Border, White Spots (BRRB).

Nasal swabs are not reliable for diagnosing pneumococcal infections; blood cultures or CSF analysis are preferred.

sections.title: Prevention
paragraphs: Mandatory preventive vaccination with a 10-valent vaccine (Synflorix) in accordance with the current vaccination schedule (for children born after January 1, 2017) or with the recommended 13-valent vaccine (Prevnar 13).

sections.title: Etiopathogenesis
paragraphs: Infection with isolated wild strains of poliovirus type 1 (epidemic type), type 2 (endemic type), and type 3 (epidemic type) (Picornaviridae).
Source of infection: A sick person or a virus carrier after an asymptomatic infection; the infection spreads mainly through the alimentary canal and droplets.
Period of contagiousness: A few days before falling ill until 6 weeks after the illness (period of virus excretion in the feces).

sections.title: Clinical Symptoms
paragraphs: Abortive form: Fever, headaches, sore throat, symptoms of respiratory and gastrointestinal inflammation.
Serous meningitis: Symptoms of meningeal infection; in 1% of cases progresses to the paralytic form (flaccid, asymmetric proximal paralysis, most often affecting the limb muscles).
Paralytic form: Three forms depending on the location of the lesions:
Acute asymmetric flaccid paralysis mainly of the proximal muscles.
Paralysis occurring with paralysis of the respiratory muscles and circulatory and respiratory failure (Landry form).
Cerebral form: Increased motor excitability, drowsiness, disturbances of consciousness.
SCB = Spinal, Cerebral, Bulbar (use as a mnemonic for the three paralytic forms).
Landry form = Respiratory paralysis + circulatory/respiratory failure (key feature to distinguish from other forms).
Before symptoms → 6 weeks post-illness (virus excretion in feces).

sections.title: Clinical Signs and Symptoms
paragraphs: Paralysis of cranial nerves, tremors and muscle spasms, aphasia, seizures.

sections.title: Complications
paragraphs: Muscle weakness, muscle atrophy (years after polio).

sections.title: Laboratory Diagnosis
paragraphs: Isolation of virus from stool sample.

sections.title: Treatment
paragraphs: Symptomatic: antipyretic, analgesic, sedative; rehabilitation procedures.

sections.title: Prevention
paragraphs: Vaccination according to the vaccination schedule (IPV).

sections.title: Vaccine-Associated Paralytic Poliomyelitis (VAPP)
paragraphs: Paralytic poliomyelitis following live attenuated vaccine (OPV) or 4–75 days after contact with a person vaccinated with OPV.

Patients who have not had contact with the environment where wild poliovirus transmission is possible and in whom no wild-type virus is detected upon double stool examination, but in which at least one attenuated strain is detected.

sections.title: Salivary Gland Inflammation (Swine Fever, Parotitis)
paragraphs: Transmission by droplet contact, rarely through saliva-contaminated objects.
🧠Memory Aid Clinical Signs Mnemonic: PAST (Paralysis, Aphasia, Seizures, Tremors).
VAPP occurs after OPV vaccination or exposure to OPV-vaccinated individuals.
Differentiate from wild polio by detecting attenuated strains (not wild-type virus) in stool.

| Vaccine Type | Risk of VAPP | Preferred for Routine Use | |--------------|--------------|---------------------------| | IPV | 0 | Yes | | OPV | 1 in 1–2.5 million | No (due to VAPP risk) | Parotitis Transmission: Remember droplet spread is the main route; avoid sharing utensils or close contact during outbreaks.

sections.title: Period of Contagiousness
paragraphs: 2–6 days before the appearance of salivary gland swelling
Up to 9 days after the onset of swelling

sections.title: Acute Symptoms
paragraphs: Painful, unilateral (most often left side) or bilateral enlargement of salivary glands
Swelling appears 7–9 days after prodromal symptoms
Elevation of the cheek associated with salivary gland swelling
Swelling under the jaw Submandibular Duct (Stensen’s duct):
Pain and redness at the duct opening Oral Symptoms:
Redness and inflammation of the mucous membrane of the throat and cheeks at the level of the premolars Saliva Production:
Increased sensitivity to sour taste Systemic Symptoms:

sections.title: Pharyngitis
paragraphs: 15–30% of cases: asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic

sections.title: Complications
paragraphs: 2. Peritonsillar Abscess (usually on the 8th day of illness; 4% of cases may cause infertility)
5. Testicular or Epididymal Inflammation, Orchitis, Oophoritis (rarely)

sections.title: Clinical Pearl
paragraphs: Peritonsillar abscess is a rare but serious complication that may lead to infertility in 4% of cases. Monitor for signs of abscess formation (e.g., trismus, unilateral swelling) on day 8 of illness.

sections.title: Treatment
paragraphs: Symptomatic: antipyretic; warm compresses to the area around the salivary glands.

sections.title: Prevention
paragraphs: Vaccination according to the vaccination schedule (Priorix, MMR).
Isolation of patients until clinical symptoms subside, for at least 9 days.

sections.title: MOLLUSCUM CONTAGIOSUM
paragraphs: Infection by Molluscum contagiosum virus (MCV - Poxvirus).
Most common in children aged 1–5 years.
Transmission through contact with an infected person or clothing, towels, toys, and other objects.

Characteristic pearl-like bumps with a depression in the central part of the lesion, localized on the skin of hands, torso, face, most commonly on the inner surfaces of the thighs, genital organs, and around the inguinal area.
When pressed, material resembling mucus is expelled from the central part of the bump.
Local signs of inflammation may appear in case of bacterial infection.
Detection of intracytoplasmic internal bodies within tissue samples (Wright's stain, Giemsa or Gram staining).
Confirmation of "molluscum bodies" under light microscopy.

sections.title: Memory Aid Scarlet Fever (Płonica, Szkarlatyna)
paragraphs: Mnemonic for clinical symptoms: "Pearl-like bumps with central pits" → "Pearly Pearls with Pits".
Transmission acronym: CLOTH (Contact, Clothing, Towels, Objects, Hands).
Key lab finding: "Molluscum bodies" (intracytoplasmic inclusions seen with Wright/Giemsa staining).
Prevention highlight: MMR vaccine (Priorix) and 9-day isolation.

sections.title: Treatment of Skin Changes in Children
paragraphs: Mechanical removal (grinding bumps after local anesthesia).
Pharmacotherapy: Rarely used in children (e.g., Imiquimod, Kantridin, Trentynoina).

sections.title: Etiopathogenesis
paragraphs: Cause: Infection with β-hemolytic group A streptococcus producing toxic erythrogenic toxin.
Droplets, direct contact with objects, and food (especially milk).
Does not occur before 1 year of age.
Presence of streptococci in maternal vaginal secretions.

sections.title: Clinical Symptoms
paragraphs: Fine papular rash (blanching or erythematous with skin indentation).
Finkelstein sign: No rash (used to differentiate from other conditions).
Pastia lines: Linear ecchymoses in superficial/joint spaces.
Hecht sign: Linear ecchymoses after injection.
Pastia lines: Remember as "Pastia" = "Past" (pastel-colored lines) on the skin.
Scarlet fever rash: "Blanching, fine, and fleeting" (blanching, fine papules, resolves in 5 days).
Tongue appearance: "Strawberry tongue" (red, bumpy, like a strawberry).
🧠Comparison Table: Scarlet Fever vs. Other Rash Conditions Feature Scarlet Fever Measles
Rash appearance Fine, blanching papules Coarse, erythematous macules
Scarlet fever is a streptococcal infection with a distinct rash and strawberry tongue. Treatment in children depends on lesion severity— wait for isolated changes, grind for recurrent ones.
- Skin peeling occurs in the 3rd week of illness, mainly on feet and hands.
- Rash areas: Skin damage from cosmetic procedures, cracked vesicles of chickenpox, etc.
- Heart muscle inflammation and pericarditis Laboratory Diagnostics
- Identification of Bordetella pertussis from throat swab (antigen rapid test)
- Mandatory: General urine examination (during illness or post-recovery) Treatment
- Transmission: Droplet infection (peak cases at age 5)
- Complications of measles: Use B.M.E.K.J. mnemonic:
